# Depth and Geometry Supervision

Also called: Geometric Regularization, Depth Priors, Geometric Constraints

## Overview
Depth and Geometry Supervision refers to a family of training procedures that incorporate explicit geometric information—such as depth maps, 3D keypoints, or structural priors—into the optimization of [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) ([NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)) and related radiance field representations. These methods solve the ambiguity between shape and appearance (the "shape-radiance ambiguity") and mitigate overfitting to sparse or textureless views by constraining the density field to align with known geometric structures [S1, S2, S4]. Unlike sibling methods that rely on semantic embeddings, diffusion priors, or stochastic structural similarity, this family explicitly leverages metric or relative depth information to regularize the volume rendering process, often accelerating convergence and reducing artifacts like "floaters" [S1, S3][S7, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate within an augmented loss structure where the [total loss](#4177-total-loss-function.md) $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}$ is a weighted sum of the standard [photometric reconstruction loss](#7799-photometric-reconstruction-loss.md) and one or more [regularization terms](#1413-regularization-losses.md) $\mathcal{L}_k$ [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{photo}} + \sum_k \lambda_k \mathcal{L}_k $$

where $\lambda_k$ are hyperparameters controlling the strength of each regularizer [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. The photometric loss is typically the [Mean Squared Error](#1651-mse-loss-and-psnr-conversion.md) (MSE) between the rendered color $\mathbf{C}$ and the ground truth image $I$:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{photo}} = || \mathbf{C} - I ||_2^2 $$

Regularization terms $\mathcal{L}_k$ operate on the density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ fields, the rendered weights $w_i$, or the final rendered images to constrain the solution space [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. Common strategies include enforcing spatial smoothness, ensuring geometric consistency across views, aligning the output distribution with learned priors, or matching semantic embeddings. The gradients of these terms are backpropagated through the [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) process to update the NeRF parameters [S1, 8582-regnerf.md].

## Subtopics

### [Geometric Baseline Regularization](7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md)
A [composite loss](#13444-overall-training-objective.md) function designed to prevent degenerate solutions in NeRF optimization, particularly in few-view settings where the model might collapse to copying training images. It augments the standard photometric loss with three geometric priors: foreground completeness (ensuring rays are fully absorbed), frustum consistency (penalizing density in only one view), and depth distribution compactness (encouraging weights to cluster around the expected depth). Choose this method when training with sparse views and no external depth priors are available.

### [Guided Optimization of NeRF](7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md)
Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in poorly textured indoor scenes by constraining the sampling range of points along camera rays using adapted monocular depth priors. It dynamically adjusts the near and far bounds of [stratified sampling](#1557-stratified-sampling.md) based on multi-view geometric consistency errors, refining the final depth output without requiring explicit depth supervision during the optimization loop. Choose this for indoor scenes with limited texture where standard sampling leads to incorrect geometry.

### [Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map](8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md)
Addresses the under-constrained optimization of reconstructing a 3D scene from a single panoramic input by initializing NeRF geometry using estimated depth maps. It explicitly performs a deformable alignment of multiple perspective depth estimates into a canonical panorama before training, resolving scale ambiguity inherent in single-view depth estimation. Choose this when only a single 360-degree image is available.

### [Depth-Supervised NeRF](8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md)
Accelerates NeRF optimization and improves quality with sparse input views by incorporating depth supervision from sparse 3D keypoints derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). It enforces that the rendered ray termination distribution matches surface priors using a KL divergence loss, making it flexible and independent of training data distribution assumptions. Choose this when sparse SfM keypoints are available but dense depth maps are not.

### [Depth Structural Consistency Regularization](9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md)
Enforces continuity constraints on rendered depth maps by leveraging external depth priors (e.g., from DepthAnythingV2). It distinguishes itself by explicitly modeling local depth variations between neighboring pixels using a k-nearest neighbors (KNN) approach with a boundary threshold, preserving sharp structural edges while smoothing noise. Choose this when high-quality monocular depth estimates are available and edge preservation is critical.

### [Novel View Regularization](10806-novel-view-regularization.md)
Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in sparse data by injecting synthetic rays into the optimization loop to provide additional geometric supervision. It explicitly guides the network toward geometrically plausible solutions by rendering and supervising views not present in the input dataset, reducing "floaters" and enforcing cross-scale consistency. Choose this when training data is extremely sparse and standard regularization fails to generalize.

### [3D Point Supervision Loss](12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md)
Minimizes the distance between learned 3D points (backprojected from rendered depth) and ground-truth 3D points, successfully registering poses in sparse-view regimes. Unlike depth-only losses, it enforces a global geometric connection between training images, preventing disjoint local solutions. Choose this when accurate 3D point clouds are available and pose refinement is required.

### [Generalized Ray Supervision](14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md)
Optimizes neural scene representations by treating arbitrary rays (e.g., shadow rays) as "ray sensors" that record incoming radiance, extending standard camera-ray supervision. It leverages physical light transport properties to constrain the density field without requiring explicit geometric labels like depth maps. Choose this when auxiliary sensor data (e.g., from light fields or shadow sensors) is available.

### [Depth Refinement and Filtering](14242-depth-refinement-and-filtering.md)
Not given in the sources.

### Coarse-Fine Consistency Loss
A loss function that enforces consistency between depth estimates of the [coarse and fine NeRF](#3406-coarse-to-fine-nerf.md) models to prevent ineffective hierarchical sampling and blur [S1]. It is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{cfc} = \mathbf{1}_{\{m_f=1\}} \odot ||z_c - \hat{\nabla}(z_f)||^2 + \mathbf{1}_{\{m_c=1\}} \odot ||\hat{\nabla}(z_c) - z_f||^2$, where $z_c$ and $z_f$ are coarse and fine depths, and $m_c/m_f$ are reliability masks determined by reprojection [S1].

### Robust Depth Loss
A loss function designed to address geometry error degradation in extrapolation performance by being less sensitive to outliers than [L2 loss](#6038-mean-square-error-mse.md), encouraging NeRF to terminate rays around pseudo depth while retaining freedom for inaccurate geometry [S2]. It is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{robust}}(\mathbf{r}) = \begin{cases} 0.5\Delta D(\mathbf{r})^{2}, &\text{if } \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) < \beta \\ \beta^{2} (0.5 + \log (\frac{\Delta D(\mathbf{r})}{\beta})), &\text{otherwise } \end{cases} $$
where $\Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - D(\mathbf{r})$ is the absolute depth difference, $\beta$ is a constant set to 0.1, and $\hat{D}(\mathbf{r})$ is the depth expectation along the camera axis of ray $r(t)$ [S2].

### Depth Supervision with Planar Architectural Depth Priors
Incorporates precomputed depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls into NeRF training to enforce geometric constraints on textureless planar surfaces [S3]. It uses MSE and BoundL losses alongside photometric loss, with a BoundL tolerance $\delta$ of 1 mm [S3]. This approach converges faster (120,000 iterations vs 200,000 for photometric-only) by concentrating sampling on occupied regions [S3].

### Indirect Depth Supervision (KL Loss)
A [regularization technique](#11314-regularization-techniques.md) that uses depth priors to constrain the NeRF weights by aligning the probability distribution of rendering weights with the depth prior, specifically using KL divergence [S4]. The loss is $L_{KL} = \sum_{i}^{N_r} \sum_{t=t_n}^{t_f} D(r_i) - \epsilon \log w_k \exp(-\frac{(t - D(r_i))^2}{2\hat{\sigma}^2}) \Delta t_k$, where $w_k$ are rendering weights and $\epsilon$ is a kernel parameter [S4].

### Geometry and Opacity Regularization
Consists of a [sparsity loss](#1203-nerf-training-configuration.md) $L_S = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} O(i)$ to suppress floaters, and an opacity loss $L_O = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} [O(i) \cdot \log(O(i)) + (1 - O(i)) \cdot \log(1 - O(i))]$ to avoid translucent effects by encouraging opacity values to be 0 or 1 [S5].

### Direct Depth Supervision
A [training objective](#8586-regularization-and-loss-functions.md) that directly compares the depth rendered by the NeRF with a ground truth depth prior using a pixel-wise loss function, such as MSE ($L_{MSE} = \sum ||D(r_i) - \hat{D}(r_i)||^2$) or L1 ($L_{L1} = \sum |D(r_i) - \hat{D}(r_i)|$) [S4].

### GeoAug
An approach that uses data augmentation by rendering new training images with new noisy camera poses using DSNeRF as a baseline and using [depth as regularization](#7616-depth-regularization.md) [S6].

### Depth Supervision
A training technique to improve reconstructed geometry by providing depth priors using off-the-shelf depth estimation models, resulting in better geometry and reduced number of floaters [S7, unofficial]. It requires refitting all depth maps against a prior point cloud to the same scale; maps that fail refitting are discarded [S7, unofficial].

## Background
The problem of shape-radiance ambiguity in NeRF optimization was identified early on, particularly in sparse-view settings where the model could overfit to training images or produce "floaters" in empty space [S1, S2]. Depth-Supervised NeRF (DS-NeRF) was one of the first methods to introduce explicit geometric constraints using sparse 3D keypoints from SfM, using a KL divergence loss to align rendered depth distributions with surface priors [S1, S4]. Subsequent work explored various forms of supervision: dense monocular depth priors [S2, S4], architectural priors for indoor scenes [S3], and consistency losses between coarse and fine hierarchical models [S1]. The field has expanded to include [generalized ray supervision](#14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md) for light transport [S14127] and 3D point-based registration [S12693], reflecting a broader trend toward integrating explicit geometric signals into implicit neural representations.
